title: One office, two responsibilities
label: 18 November 2026 · The Lord Advocate’s dual role
summary: The committee asked former Lord Advocate Lord Mulholland whether Scotland’s senior prosecutor should also advise the Government. He argued that the combination helps prosecutors warn ministers about live investigations and brings prosecution experience into government decisions and new laws. He said he had never experienced political interference, but acknowledged that the public may worry about conflicts of interest. Members challenged whether safeguards and recusal from some cases make the arrangement look unusual; Mulholland said the system works, while supporting written guidance on when Law Officers should step aside. He also discussed appointments, public transparency, the office’s wide-ranging duties and the pressure of the job.

glossary.definition: Scotland’s senior legal officer, who advises the Scottish Government and leads the independent prosecution service.
The Lord Advocate’s deputy and another senior legal officer in Scotland.
Senior prosecutors who advise on and make decisions about serious criminal cases.
To step aside from a decision because involvement could appear unfair or conflicted.
A rule limiting public discussion of a case while court proceedings are under way.
Making a decision under legal rules in a way that should be independent of party politics.
The law that established Scotland’s devolved Parliament and Government and sets out their powers.

glossary.term: Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service
glossary.definition: Scotland’s prosecution service, which investigates deaths and brings criminal cases to court.

chapters.title: Why combine the roles?
chapters.takeaway: Mulholland said one person overseeing prosecutions and advising ministers can help protect investigations and improve government decisions.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are the main advantages of the Lord Advocate being both the Government’s legal adviser and Scotland’s senior prosecutor?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: The combination helps ministers understand what they can safely say during a major investigation. After the Glasgow airport bombing and the Clutha helicopter crash, politicians needed to reassure the public, but also avoid saying anything that could damage an inquiry. A prosecutor can explain where those boundaries are.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: It also lets the Lord Advocate spot problems in the justice system and raise them with Government. In one terrorism investigation, differences between Scottish and English legal time limits complicated efforts to prosecute connected cases together. I raised the problem with the UK Government, and a change was made to allow certain terrorism crimes to be prosecuted across the UK.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I also raised the lack of a Scottish law covering the sharing of intimate images without consent. There are other examples where a prosecutor’s experience can help ministers consider new laws.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: The Lockerbie investigation is another example. I reviewed the case papers and publicly said I believed the conviction was sound. The FBI director then contacted me, and we went to Libya after Gaddafi’s fall to discuss pursuing others who might have been involved. The First Minister needed to know about the trip because it was dangerous and could have become major international news.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So you see practical benefits for both prosecution work and the development of government policy?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: Yes. I could give many more examples. I’m not saying ministers should be told the evidence in a live case; they may need to know what is happening so they can govern responsibly.

chapters.title: Political independence and public confidence
chapters.takeaway: Mulholland said the risk is that people may suspect political influence, but he saw no such interference in his own work.

turns.speaker: Lillian Jones
turns.text: What are the risks of combining the roles?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: The biggest risk is that people think the prosecutor has political motives. Historically, Lords Advocate sometimes took part in political prosecutions. But the office has changed, and Dame Elish Angiolini made a point of keeping the prosecution service’s budget separate from the Government’s justice budget, to help protect its independence.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: The Scotland Act 1998 also protects the Lord Advocate’s independent decisions about prosecutions and investigations into deaths. In my nine years as a Law Officer, no minister, MSP, MP or First Minister ever asked me to discuss evidence in a live case.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: Ministers sometimes make decisions that must be taken under legal rules rather than party politics. A planning decision or a decision about an energy project can be quasi-judicial. I believe the Lord Advocate can also keep the prosecutor’s role separate from political work.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: During the independence referendum, I gave the Government legal advice on whether the Scottish Parliament could hold a referendum. I was determined that the result would have a sound legal basis, whichever way people voted.

turns.speaker: Dave Doogan
turns.text: Some people worry that being in Government meetings gives ministers access to information about cases they shouldn’t have. Is it frustrating that people assume information will leak, when you say that simply wouldn’t happen?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: It is frustrating, but there was no leakage of criminal-case information during my time. The Lord Advocate doesn’t routinely attend Cabinet. I went to about one in four Government Cabinet meetings, depending on the agenda, and never attended the separate political meetings.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I attended when ministers needed legal advice or guidance about an inquiry. For example, I once challenged an estimate of inquiry costs that I thought was far too low. I also advised ministers on what they could say during live investigations.

turns.speaker: Mr MacDonald
turns.text: On balance, should the two roles be split?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: No. You would lose the prosecutor’s input into government policy and legislation, and the ability to warn ministers when their public comments could prejudice an inquiry.

chapters.title: Recusal and the appearance of a conflict
chapters.takeaway: Members questioned whether stepping aside from some cases shows a weakness in the dual role; Mulholland said it is a limited safeguard, not proof of interference.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: There are cases where neither the Lord Advocate nor Solicitor General makes the prosecution decision, but one of them may still have to answer questions in Parliament. Could that seem strange to the public?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: If a case involves an MSP or MP, the usual practice is for the Law Officers to step aside. An independent Crown Counsel makes the decision instead. A Law Officer may still need a briefing to answer Parliament, including an explanation of why they can’t discuss something.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: Isn’t that the difficulty with the dual role? Even if there’s no actual interference, the possibility of a reasonable person suspecting a conflict means the Lord Advocate may have to step aside.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I’m aware of the convention applying to cases involving an MSP or MP. In my experience, I never had political interference and never discussed live cases with politicians. In a case involving an MSP, the decision went to independent Crown Counsel.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: I’m not suggesting you’d interfere. But having to send a case elsewhere to avoid the appearance of a conflict is itself a consequence of combining the roles.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I understand that concern. But a request for a judge to step aside doesn’t mean the judge must do so. I once prosecuted a case where the judge faced such a request and refused it. In another situation, I didn’t believe I needed to step aside, but decided someone else could make the decision.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: Are there formal safeguards to prevent political interference?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: There are legal protections and established procedures. The Crown Office has experienced staff who brief the Law Officers on what they can and can’t do, especially in high-profile cases. The organisation has a strong culture of independent prosecution decisions.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: But things can go wrong. Wouldn’t splitting the roles add oversight?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I’m not sure what that extra oversight would be. The law and existing procedures protect decisions, and I don’t think splitting the roles would necessarily change public perceptions. I wasn’t involved in the Peter Murrell case, but I have no reason to doubt that its decision was made without political interference.

chapters.title: What ministers are told
chapters.takeaway: Mulholland distinguished between alerting ministers to a public-interest issue and giving them details or evidence from a criminal case.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: Did you ever experience or face an attempt at political interference?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: No. MSPs asked about the investigation into losses from an RBS share issue. I explained its process and likely timetable, but nobody asked me about the evidence or allegations. I also warned them that public comment could affect the case.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: Were your conversations with the First Minister always formally recorded?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: No. Sometimes we spoke informally, but not about live cases. Formal requests for legal advice would be put in writing, and the advice would be written too. Before a sensitive trip to Libya, I spoke to the First Minister rather than put details in writing, because I feared a document might leak.

turns.speaker: Lillian Jones
turns.text: You were Lord Advocate when Andrew Coulson was prosecuted for perjury. How did you keep that case free from political influence?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: Crown Counsel made the decision and prosecuted the case. I had no reason to interfere and wasn’t involved in the decision. The trial judge later ruled there was no case to answer under the law on perjury.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I also wrote to the Presiding Officer, the Commons Speaker and the Prime Minister because I feared public comments might prejudice the case. I didn’t decide the prosecution, but the warning came from a Law Officer. The letters didn’t discuss the evidence, and there was no public comment.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: That seems different from the message sent by the current Lord Advocate to the First Minister about the Murrell case, which reportedly included more detail.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I haven’t researched that case. I understand the decision was made by independent Crown Counsel, but you’d need to ask the current Lord Advocate why she sent the message in those terms.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Did you ever tell ministers details such as the amount of money involved or the progress of a live prosecution?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I can think of one case where I told ministers an application was about to be made to reopen the World’s End murder case. That followed a change in the law allowing some acquittals to be reconsidered when new evidence emerged. I didn’t explain the evidence or why it met the test; the application would shortly become public.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I don’t recall sending ministers a message about the MSP prosecution I mentioned. I answered questions about it in Parliament, but I can’t say for certain whether any update was sent.

chapters.title: Making the rules clearer
chapters.takeaway: Mulholland supported publishing more guidance, especially about when a Law Officer should step aside from a case.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Crown Office recently introduced public statements explaining its practices. Is that new?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: It’s a new policy, although prosecution guidance has been published before on particular issues. I support telling the public what factors prosecutors consider, including in cases involving young people or sexual offences.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: Would it help to write down the rules for when the Lord Advocate or Solicitor General steps aside?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: Yes. The convention is unwritten, and putting it on paper could help the public understand it. It would be worth considering exactly who it covers: sitting MSPs and MPs, former members, or people in other senior political roles. That needs careful thought, and the current Lord Advocate should be asked too.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: Would formalising every conversation between the Lord Advocate and First Minister also help?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: In my view, that would go too far and could make good government harder. We sometimes need to speak quickly. For instance, after the First Minister criticised a court decision on television, I went to see him and told him not to criticise judges. It helped calm the situation. That conversation concerned prosecution responsibilities, not my role as Government legal adviser.

turns.speaker: Lillian Jones
turns.text: If the roles were split, would the Government benefit from having a party-political legal adviser, as happens in the UK and Welsh Governments?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I don’t think so. A lawyer who belongs to the governing party could feel pressure to give advice the Government wants to hear. The Government needs candid advice about whether a plan is legal and, if not, what would need to change. The referendum question showed how important that independence can be.

chapters.title: Appointments, duties and workload
chapters.takeaway: Mulholland favoured politically independent Law Officers, saw value in experience but not a single required career path, and described a demanding office with a broad remit.

turns.speaker: Lillian Jones
turns.text: What are the benefits and drawbacks of appointing a Lord Advocate on a non-political basis?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I’ve never made my political views public, and neither Alex Salmond nor Nicola Sturgeon asked me about them. In my view, not belonging to a political party helps protect the independence of the job. If the roles were split and the Government appointed a political legal adviser, the advice might be less candid.

turns.speaker: Lillian Jones
turns.text: Should a Lord Advocate be barred from serving as an MSP?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I saw the job as serving both the Scottish Parliament and the UK Parliament. Scotland’s prosecutors also deal with matters such as terrorism, firearms and drugs, which cross the boundaries between devolved and UK responsibilities.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: Would a more open, competitive appointment process give the public greater confidence?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: You may have a point. I was asked unexpectedly to become Solicitor General after years as a prosecutor and a senior prosecutor in Edinburgh. Later, I was asked to become Lord Advocate. I was interviewed for the first job, but I don’t think there were other candidates.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: Should the appointee have to be a career prosecutor?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: No. Experience helps, but the role needs hard work, sound judgment and strong principles; there isn’t only one suitable career path. As Lord Advocate, I set up a unit to review unsolved murders. I’d been shocked to learn there were more than 500 unsolved homicides, and I hoped success would mean solving even one. The work has since led to several cases being resolved.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: Should the Lord Advocate normally serve for no more than five years?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I stepped down after nine years because the work was taking a toll on my health. It was an exceptionally demanding job, especially through the referendum and major events such as the Clutha crash and terrorist investigations.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: Would the job be healthier without the dual role?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I don’t agree, but the decision is for Parliament. I’m giving you my experience, not speaking for the courts.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Would the job be harder without a Solicitor General to help?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: Yes. The Solicitor General can act when the Lord Advocate is away and can help prepare someone for the top job. I sometimes made around 50 important decisions in a day. The Lord Advocate also has wider duties, including protecting the public interest, giving prosecution guidance and setting priorities—for example, my guidance called for knife possession in public to be prosecuted except in very unusual circumstances. I believe homicide numbers later fell substantially, though I can’t attribute that change to one measure alone.
